#9842. Reversing the Next-Page Prefetcher in Skylake-X

Intel publishes very little about next-page prefetchers in their P-cores. Back in the Ivy Bridge days, it was known that IVB included a next-page prefetcher thanks to this ancient excerpt from an old copy of the Intel Architectures Optimization Reference Manual:

Hardware prefetch enhancement: A next-page prefetcher (NPP) is added in Intel microarchitecture code name Ivy Bridge. The NPP is triggered by sequential accesses to cache lines approaching the page boundary, either upwards or downwards.

A recent issue of the optimization manual states that Redwood Cove includes a Last Level Cache (LLC) Page Prefetcher which is like NPP but with a slightly more sophisticated prefetch algorithm:

The LLC Page Prefetcher extends the Next-Page-Prefetcher algorithm, which detects a sequence of accesses that are about to reach the end of a page (either going up towards the next page in memory or down towards the previous page in memory) and triggers a linear prefetch to the start of the next predicted page. NPP intends to prefetch the translation of the next page and initiate prefetching of the first few cache lines from that predicted page. The LLC Page Prefetch enhances Next-Page Prefetcher in two significant ways:

Redwood Cove is a relatively recent microarchitecture which shipped in Meteor Lake P-cores starting late 2023. Ivy Bridge on the other hand is very old; It launched back in 2012 and was discontinued by 2015 right before Skylake launched. That raises the question, what happened in-between? Did every microarchitecture after IVB include a next-page prefetcher?

It’s unlikely that the details remain unchanged from one microarchitecture to the next but as it turns out, I recently got unlimited access to a Skylake-X machine that I didn’t have to pay a single dime for. Given the setup, it’s only natural I got nerd-sniped into reversing the next-page prefetcher…and that’s what this post is about. I hope you enjoy it!

Hardware component that preloads data that the program might need soon. The goal is to eliminate memory stalls when the CPU actually demands the piece of data that the prefetcher could have loaded earlier. All kinds of prefetchers exist in modern CPUs. Next-Line prefetchers prefetch the immediate next cache line when the N’th cache line is accessed. Stride prefetchers (usually IP-based) track the stride of consecutive memory accesses that originate from the same instruction and if the access pattern turns out to be regular enough, it eagerly initiates the load from address that it predicted. Next-Page Prefetchers preload page table entries into the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) provided software traverses memory pages in predictable manner. These by no means are the only three kind; a high-performance CPU may implement many other types of prefetchers, some of which are documented in this Intel whitepaper.

Prefetchers that are required to act fast are logically simple and tend not to cross page boundaries because that may complicate things with, e.g. page faults and page walks on TLB misses. For example, the next-line prefetcher is supposed to fetch the next cache line if the accesses are sequential, but if the next cache line sits in a different page it may decide not to prefetch at all. Next-page prefetchers are slightly different in that regard; they prefetch the next page table entry (PTE) into the TLB. They have to work across page boundaries by design.

In this post I’ll try to answer the following questions:

But before we start, let’s prepare the stage for our experiments.

If you don’t intend to run the experiments described in this post, you can skip this part.

Documenting the many details of performance monitoring on various platforms deserves a post of its own, and a fairly long one at that. For simplicity I’m only going to focus on Linux. Linux allows configuring performance monitoring events via the perf_event_open syscall. That’s what I’ll be using in my experiments too but generally speaking, you don’t need special system APIs to access PMU counters. At least on Intel, you only need some way of writing a set of performance monitoring MSRs (usually only the IA32_PERFEVTSELx MSRs) and read the counters back from a set of corresponding IA32_PMCx MSRs. WRMSR and RDMSR require Ring0 access so if you’re on Windows, you’d have to write a kernel-mode driver and use __readmsr/__writemsr intrinsics to read/write the relevant MSRs. That said, the hard part of making custom drivers for Windows isn’t writing the driver itself, rather convincing the kernel to load your driver. More on that in a future blog post.

Performance monitoring tools that allow reading PMU counters (e.g. perf, VTune) may also work. I’d stick to perf_event_open because it allows better control over the exact segment of code I need to measure. The manpage includes an example of how to use perf_event_open. For our experiments we need three things in order:

We’ll write a helper for each of these steps: configure_event_group to configure the events, start_counters to enable the counters, and stop_counters to stop and read the counters. With that aside, here’s configure_event_group:

Full source code of every experiment, data structure, and helpers used in this article can be found on github. The group_fd identifies the event group that you configure via perf_event_open. You can use that group_fd to perform certain operations on the event group, like enabling or disabling the counters. That’s what we’re going to do next: enable the counters with start_counters which is defined like this:

Calling start_counters sets off the counters for every event configured in the event group identified by group_fd. At this point we’ll run our workload, then call stop_counters to stop and read the counters:

Before we can read PMU counters using the functions defined above, we need to tweak some settings on Linux. Depending on your distro, certain restrictions may apply by default on hardware PMU access due to security reasons. You can overcome them by setting perf_event_paranoid to 0 or -1:

You may also need to disable THP and pin the calling thread to a core if there’s too much going on in your machine.

Now we have all the pieces required to start monitoring hardware events. Throughout this post we’d work with the following events:

It’s note hard to observe that the event configs are of the form 0x, where Umask and EventSel are coming straight from the “PROGRAMMING INFO” column of the corresponding event in the perfmon website (the ‘H’ suffix is Intel’s way of saying the number is given in hexadecimal). Not all event configs are derived this way, but it’s enough for the simple ones we’re gonna use here.

SKX (codename for Skylake-X) has two TLB levels: L1 and L2. Each SKX core gets a physically separate L1 data TLB (dTLB) and L1 instruction TLB (iTLB). The L2 TLB (also called Second Level TLB or STLB) is unified, i.e. both instruction and data PTEs go to the same STLB.

Both L1 and L2 TLBs are partitioned based on the page size. L1 dTLB has a total of 100 entries: 64 reserved for 4k pages, 32 for 2M or 4M pages, and 4 for 1G pages. The dTLB is 4-way set associative so each set can hold 4 page-table entries. The iTLB is also partitioned: has 128 entries for 4k pages, 16 entries for 2M or 4M pages, and none for 1G pages. The STLB has 1536 entries shared between 4k and 2M pages and an additional 16 entries for 1G huge pages. STLB is not inclusive of the L1 TLBs. That means at any given instance, a page-table entry may exist in one of the L1 TLBs, the STLB, or both.

For the purposes of this post, we don’t need to dig any further into the geometry of SKX TLBs. It’s time to run some experiments!

The very first question that we should ask is whether the next-page prefetcher exists in SKX at all. NPPs seem like a good idea in general; given that Intel had the silicon budget to include one in Ivy Bridge, we expect the answer to be “Yes” in SKX too. To test this, we’ll design a workload that walks a mapped range of 1000 4K pages sequentially and measure how many TLB misses we get. I cannot imagine a more favourable access pattern for the NPP to kick in if it truly exists. If the workload below doesn’t trigger the prefetcher, we can safely conclude that SKX doesn’t have one.

Not much going on here. We have a function that touches every byte in the mapped range starting at MAP_BASE. The seemingly useless zero helps ensure that loads from the mapped range execute serially. Take a closer look at how we’re using zero in the loop. Loading the next byte from the mapped range at iteration i depends on the value of zero computed at iteration i-1. Computing zero at iteration i-1 in turn depends on computing dummy at iteration i-1. We have a cyclic loop-carried dependency chain here: the load in map_base[i + zero] feeds add in dummy += .... The result of that add then feeds the and in zero = zero & .... Result of the and feeds the next load at iteration i+1. In layman terms, the loads at iteration i and iteration i+1 cannot execute together or out-of-order. This is intentional: alloweing out-of-order execution of the two loads could significantly perturb our results. We’ll see why in a moment.

The last line is a common trick to avoid the compiler throw away our computation; it’s falsely advertising that the inline asm uses the value of dummy computed in the loop and forcing the compiler to materialize dummy into a register.

Nice. A few instructions here and there but we got the loop compiled exactly how we wanted. Note that the dependency chain we just discussed translates exactly to assembly too. Running the workload gives the following count for the two events:

Over a few runs DTLB_LOAD_MISSES.STLB_HIT fluctuates between the 50..75 band, but never exceeds 75. That’s already interesting: we walked through 1000 pages in the loop but DTLB_LOAD_MISSES.STLB_HIT is nowhere near 1000. DTLB_LOAD_MISSES.STLB_HIT = 70 means only 70 out of the 1000 PTE requests missed in dTLB and hit STLB. The obvious next question is what happened to rest of the 1000 - 70 = 930 fresh PTE requests that the loop might have initiated? There are two possible answers:

We can quickly rule out (1) because MEM_INST_RETIRED.STLB_MISS_LOADS = 1. So that leaves us with (2): about 930 new PTE requests hit in the dTLB when the demand arrived. But that must mean that SKX has a prefetcher that’s prefilling the dTLB with future PTEs. Yep! It’s the next-page prefetcher in action. Well, strictly speaking this could also be a non-NPP prefetcher that is allowed prefetch beyond page boundaries but as they say, if it quacks like a duck, it’s the next-page prefetcher!

Subtle point that is easy to miss: the prefetcher is loading entries into th dTLB. This doesn’t automatically prove or disprove that it’s also prefilling STLB. In SKX the STLB acts as a victim cache, i.e. entries that are evicted from L1 TLBs are stored in the STLB. Thinking along those lines, it doesn’t make much sense for the prefetcher to prefill the STLB too, but I’d refrain from such speculations. Perhaps a carefully designed experiment can unveil that secret, but that’s not my focus in this post. We’d also not worry about the iTLB for now.

Microarchitecture explorations typically require careful use of statistics to extract signal buried in noise. Luckily in this case the signal is so strong that we can get away with sloppiness.

Alright, we have established that SKX has a next-page prefetcher that prefills the dTLB. On to the next question!

Something in the loop in touch_all_bytes must have triggered the next-page prefetch. The most obvious guess is a load from the previous page. Question is, which load? Is it just a single load from a special offset? A set of loads? There are so many questions that could be asked here…we need an experiment that narrows down the space of possibilities. We can imagine a workload that touches only the left half of each page (bytes in the range page[0..2047], inclusive) and count the TLB misses. If we still see TLB miss numbers like in our first experiment, that’d mean accesses from the left half of the page triggers the prefetch. If we instead see TLB misses that add up to 1000 (or more), we can repeat the same experiment but this time touching the right half of the page (bytes in the range page[2048..4095], inclusive). A generic workload that accepts an offset and a slice_length can handle both cases:

When touch_page_slice is called with offset = 0, slice_length = 2048, it walks left half of each of the 1000 mapped pages. Walking the right half is just as simple, just call touch_page_slice with offset = 2048 and slice_length = 2048. Results from walking the left half:

Walking the left half generated MEM_INST_RETIRED.STLB_MISS_LOADS = 1001. That’s suspiciously close to the total number of pages we walked! The most sensible explanation is that the NPP did not trigger while walking the left half, thus every new PTE request missed in the dTLB. Those misses then made it to STLB and then missed there too.

Alright, what about the right half? Here’s the result from waking the right half:

Comparatively, walking the right half is not bad at all. In fact this time the prefetcher clearly did trigger. We can keep splitting the slice that triggers prefetch binary-search style and further narrow the access range. The table below shows the results:

Hmm, neither left nor right slice of the last row triggers the prefetcher. But we do know that walking page[3328..3455] does work. So here’s the new plan: we start our walk at offset 3328 but not stop at 3391, rather keep pushing the right edge one byte at a time until we cause the prefetcher to trigger. For example, we’d walk page[3328..3392] and if that didn’t trigger NPP, we’d walk page[3328..3393] and so forth. We expect that the prefetcher would trigger before we reach page[3328..3455]. We can reuse touch_page_slice here too; just call it with offset = 3328 and slice_length = 65,66,....

It doesn’t take long to identify the slice that triggers prefetch: the sneaky page[3328..3392]. Calling touch_page_slice with offset = 3328 and slice_length = 65 immediately triggers the prefetch. If you’re into this kind of shannonigans, it shouldn’t take too long to notice that 3392 is the first byte into the 53rd cache line (counting zero-indexed) within a page. Ok, does that mean accessing the 53rd cache line triggers the prefetch? But that can’t be true because we accessed every single byte in the 53rd line and verified no prefetches (see “Right half” of the last row in the table). Moreover, offset 3328 starts the 52nd cache line (counting zero-indexed) within a page, so we also know that accessing every byte in the 52nd cache line also doesn’t trigger the prefetch (see the “Left half” of the last row in the table). Could it be that for the prefetcher to trigger, subsequent loads must cross the 52nd cache line into the 53rd cache line? If the prefetch condition truly is as simple as “two subsequent loads, one from cache line 52, the next from cache line 53”, then the following must hold:

To test these hypotheses, we need a workload that touches every byte in a page except a few. This should work:

The strange looking trick to compute idx in the inner loop helps avoid a branch in the probe path. Yeah, we are also banking on the fact that the branch predictor would do just fine when we’re done walking a page in the inner loop and jump back to the outer loop. Strictly speaking, a branch mispredict shouldn’t mess with TLBs in a way that affects our results but in general, eliminating noise sources to the best of your ability is a good idea with these kind of experiments. Aside from that there’s not much going on here. We are skipping the range page[hole_offset, hole_offset+hole_length] and touching every other byte in the page. When i falls within the skipped range, we simply redirect the load to hole_offset - 1.

Ok so what are the results if we skip cache line 52 and 53, i.e. range page[3328, 3391] and page[3392, 3456]:

MEM_INST_RETIRED.STLB_MISS_LOADS = 1000 for both cases. This verifies (1) and (2) from our list of hypotheses. We can test (3) by calling touch_page_slice with offset = 3391 and slice_length = 2. Here are the results:

As expected, merely touching a single byte in each of 52nd and 53rd cache lines engages the prefetcher. Now admittedly the experiment doesn’t prove the “any byte in either cache line” part; we’ve only shown that loading last byte in cache line 52 followed by the load of first byte in cache line 53 triggers the prefetch, but you can easily verify that by tweaking the parameters of touch_page_with_hole. For example, hole_offset = 3329 and hole_length = 126 touches first byte of line 52 and last byte of line 53, skipping everything in-between. This still triggers prefetch. To limit the size of this post, I’ll leave out certain details like that from here on after. I’d be happy to fill those gaps in the comment section if you have questions.

Note that for the prefetcher to trigger, load from 52nd cache line must execute before the load from 53rd cache line (unless the prefetcher is bidirectional, but we’ll get to that in a minute). This is why it was crucial to introduce the dependency chain that throttles out-of-order execution of loads from the page.

If you’re wondering why would Intel design the prefetcher with such a thin trigger condition, you’re not alone. I had the same exact question. I mean, triggering prefetch when loads get closer and closer to the next page makes sense. But why put all your bets on crossing just the 52nd cache line?! It’d make more sense if any couple of accesses beyond a threshold triggered the prefetch. Peter Cordes (yeah, that Peter Cordes) had a brilliant answer on why this makes sense. Go read it if you’re interested.

Good question. Our experiments so far have only used loads. A sane person would think stores shouldn’t behave any different. But to my surprise, stores don’t seem to trigger prefetches. If you’re browsing the full source on GitHub you’d notice that we are faulting the mapped range with loads. That choice is deliberate: we’re intentionally mapping every virtual page in the mapped range to the physical zero page. This reduces cache footprint, and potentially restricts one more source of noise.

We cannot keep doing this for this next experiment, though; we don’t want page faults in the probe path. So we switch to faulting with stores before we start the experiment. That out of the way, here’s the kernel we’ll use to verify no prefetch on stores:

Running this produces MEM_INST_RETIRED.STLB_MISS_STORES = 1000. Note that this time we are measuring STLB misses on stores. You can verify that each of these misses start at least one page-walk by counting DTLB_STORE_MISSES.WALK_COMPLETED along with MEM_INST_RETIRED.STLB_MISS_STORES. That rules out the possibility of dTLB hits and a last-level TLB (other than STLB) catching all the misses from STLB.

We have established that the next-page prefetcher prefetches at least one future PTE. We shouldn’t expect it to load more than one page ahead; it’s called next-page prefetcher for a reason. But let’s verify that with this simple workload so that there are no doubts:

The idea is to “heat up” the prefetcher by crossing 52nd cache line in the first poke_limit pages — that’s what the first loop does — then load first byte of future_limit pages beyond poke_limit in the second loop. We’ll call this function repeatedly, each time increasing future_limit by 1, and count the TLB misses. We can get a baseline with future_limit = 0 first:

Over many runs, STLB miss baseline fluctuates between 1 and 3 but never seems to exceed 3. Alright, we can work with that. Now let’s try future_limit = 1:

Yep, expected! The last load in the “heater” must’ve triggered the prefetch for page at poke_limit, so future_limit = 1 shouldn’t increase the number of observed misses. What about future_limit = 2?

Looks like the NPP prefetches only one page ahead. Cool, no complaints there!

Does the prefetcher work in backward direction too? This is the last piece of the puzzle and fortunately very easy to test: just walk the mapped range backwards. If you get close to 1000 misses the answer is no, otherwise yes. Here’s the workload:

This is a bit shocking. If you recall from the “Introduction” section, Intel manuals seem to suggest the next-page prefetcher triggers while walking “upwards” (what I call forward) or “downward” (what I call backward). This behavior is documented for both Ivy Bridge and Redwood Cove…but that’s not what we see for SKX. I don’t have any theories explaining this disconnect between SKX and the other uarchs, if you do feel free to share in the comment section.

If you’re a software developer looking for a cool new way of optimizing program performance, probably nowhere. Optimizing programs for a single microarchitecture from a single CPU vendor is almost always a bad idea for anything with half-life beyond next Friday. My goal here is to share how I attempt reversing undocumented machine behavior and invite fellow nerds to kick-start discussions that hopefully help me or somebody else learn something new.

That said, if you’re one of those weirdos who can manage to care only about one type of machine (Skylake-X to be precise), you may find the details interesting from a practical PoV. Either way, I’m tired. This is too much writing for a first post. 👋

#9841. AI found more critical bugs in another widely used technology running 225M websites

Hot on the heels of serious vulnerabilities in seemingly every other widely used software powering the entire internet, F5 today released emergency patches for 10 bugs in open source NGINX.

These include critical remote code execution flaws that let attackers hijack NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled, as well as the millions of websites running NGINX, to steal sensitive data and disrupt services.

“At this time, we have found no evidence of active exploitation of any of these vulnerabilities in the wild,” and F5 spokesperson told The Register. “We continue to monitor closely and will share updates via myF5 as we learn more.”

As with all of the other recently disclosed vulnerabilities in foundational technologies like PHP, Apache, and Java, these critical NGINX bugs were uncovered by researchers using AI. One of them has been hiding in the code for at least 10 years.

Tomer Schwartz, Wiz’s chief technology officer of exposure management and AppSec, helped find the bug, along with researchers from Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint working independently.

Schwartz told The Register that this wave of AI-discovered flaws “point to a new reality.”

“We need to treat every internet-connected system as potentially vulnerable,” Schwartz said. “AI has changed not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.”

NGINX is the world’s most widely used open source web server, handling HTTPS requests and routing incoming traffic to the right application or API. It powers about a third of all websites (around 225 million), and F5 maintains the open source version.

On Wednesday, F5 published an out-of-band security notification that addressed 10 CVEs in open source NGINIX. If you run NGINX, update to 1.31.9 as soon as possible.

Two of the vulns are especially serious as they allow a remote attacker to execute code on the NGINX server without authentication. These two, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, both received a critical, 9.2 CVSS rating, and CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.  Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server.

All of the security shops listed earlier independently found at least one of these two CVEs - most, if not all, with an AI assist - and reported them to F5.

“Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic,” Schwartz and fellow Wiz kid Nir Ohfeld said in a Wednesday blog about the two bugs. “In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy.”

Rapid7’s team also published a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated remote code execution against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8.

Xint found three other NGINX flaws, plus a separate vulnerability in the Linux kernel that can be chained with any of the five NGINX vulnerabilities to gain root privileges on the host. The research team dubbed the six bugs “nginx2root.”

The AI-powered offensive security firm also published videos demonstrating attacks using CVE-2026-123007 to execute commands as the NGINX worker inside a container, and then using the kernel vulnerability to escalate to root on the host. These attacks work on AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, and bare-metal servers.

"While preparing for ZeroDay Cloud 2026, a Xint researcher found CVE-2026-123007," the company said in a Wednesday blog. "A few days later, a fully automated Xint scan found the other four without human guidance."

All of these newly-disclosed CVEs point to a larger security issue - especially in light of Tuesday’s Java4Shell, found by AI-bug-hunting-outfit Calif, PHP2Shell (Calif was one of the firms that also used AI to find and weaponize these critical vulns in PHP), and a critical Apache flaw under active exploitation .

“AI is also accelerating vulnerability discovery faster than existing infrastructure was designed to absorb,” Schwartz told us. “Even after a vendor ships a fix, security teams still face heavy manual work in terms of locating vulnerable versions and configurations, testing patches, deploying interim mitigations (such as disabling HTTP/2), and coordinating all of these rollouts.”

There is light at the end of the tunnel, he believes. “In the long run, AI-powered vulnerability research will harden foundational software.”

But in the meantime, it’s a nightmare for security teams, vulnerability managers, and system administrators, who are drowning in the near-daily deluge of CVEs to patch before attackers find and exploit these vulnerabilities.

“Continued collaboration between security researchers, maintainers, and defenders is crucial to absorb the speed and scale of these disclosures,” Schwartz said.®

#9840. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

#9839. Phrack 73

Last year marked the 40th anniversary of Phrack so we went big. We publishedour anniversary launch release in print at Defcon 33, HOPE, WHY25 and someadditional variations at several conferences around the world includingAlligatorCon, B-Sides Canberra, Out of the Box, Datenspuren, DistrictCon,OffensiveCon, Recon, and Toorcamp. We included a CTF with exploit challengesand had puzzles and easter eggs included in the zine. We threw parties andhad talks at Defcon and WHY25 to celebrate this milestone.

More importantly, we got new research into people's hands. The point of therelaunch was to get people reading, researching, writing, and contributingagain. We wanted the next person picking up Phrack to find something thatmade them sit down at a computer and start pulling a system apart.

We owe a huge thanks to the authors, editors, artists, publishing partners,donors, and staff who made it happen. Writing the paper, working throughrevisions, putting the print editions together, paying the bills, andgetting boxes of zines to the right places all take time and effort. Most ofthat work is invisible when you are holding the finished issue. Weappreciate everyone who did it.

And to the readers: thank you for giving a shit. Seeing someone get excitedabout an article, connect it to something they are working on, or realizethat they could contribute something themselves makes the effort worthwhile.That exchange is how this thing keeps going. The relaunch worked, and thisissue is the follow-through.

This is the third release curated by the new staff, and we are not slowingdown. This issue is larger than last year's, with 23 main papers and eightadditional articles in Line Noise. The subjects range from exploitation andreverse engineering to machine learning, hardware, and the history andculture that grew around this work.

We have container escapes through the vDSO, use-after-free exploitation, QNXuserland shellcode, Linux kernel research, and a Chromium renderer sandboxescape through Skia. Elsewhere, the issue takes on Windows smart cardarchitecture, static taint analysis in Binary Ninja, and autonomousunderwater vehicles.  There is also work examining backdoors in machinelearning and what it means to trust an AI system. One paper takes us fromPhrackCTF to two WinFSP zero-days, which is a pretty good argument forcontinuing to put challenges in a zine.

We also have four more articles in Phrack World History, including the storyof the infamous SSH1 CRC32 vulnerability featured in The Matrix Reloaded aswell as stories about blue boxing free phone calls, a confession of a hackerwho tried to backdoor Linux kernel in 2003, and an early discovery ofbotnets for hire. Our Prophile features Halvar Flake, whose contributions toreverse engineering and security research are legendary.

In 2026, we find ourselves in a time of rapid technological change. It ishard to say what vulnerability research or red teaming will look like inanother five years. AI has moved well beyond completing a line of code intoagentic systems capable of analyzing source code and reverse engineeringbinaries to find and exploit vulnerabilities.

We can be sure that the future will require us to continue to explore newideas, create new tools, and push the boundaries of what is possible in theface of new challenges and opportunities created by the advancement of AIand automation systems. As the effort required to put ideas into practicefalls, creativity and human intuition forged through experience is valuedeven higher.

We hope that this release of Phrack will inspire new ideas, discussions, andcollaborations that will keep the human side of hacking a critical elementin shaping the future of technology and society. We will continue to do ourpart to support the community and provide a platform for sharing knowledgeand ideas. We look forward to seeing what the future holds and we areexcited to be a part of it.

Read the papers, try the ideas, and challenge the conclusions. When you findsomething worth sharing, write it up and send it in. We have another issueto put together, and some of you should be in it!

To those who have supported us the past three years helping to restorevitality to Phrack, we thank you.

Conferences who funded prints: Defcon, OffensiveCon, Recon, Unprompted[AU],Unprompted[US], BSides Canberra, Alligatorcon, TenguCon

Sponsors & Major Donors - WatchTowr, Elltam, Verichains, BShield,TrustedSec, Binarly, Trenchant, Praetorian (WWSUL), EFF, Blaze, EMX,Mullvad, ToorCon, Hacker Initiative, Endrazine, Dug Song, Napster, halvar,Horizon, Huku, Julio Auto, Gadi, and the rest of the people who stepped up withsmaller donations.

Artists - Ian Dash, pinguino, tainted, pepper, mar, xer0, abstrakt, ToscaKaiser,h7, zir, Mick, p0rtL, netspooky, ackmage, digitalis, Tedsig42, and the manyothers who submitted their work for consideration.

Reviewers - barbie, bsdaemon, C, chompie, danielcuthbert, devinc, grugq, joern,jordan9001, K3, richinseattle, roddux, saber, skyper, SSHad0w, TMZ, zh4ck

All the authors past and present who are now bound to the history of phrack.

All information in Phrack Magazine is, to the best of the ability ofthe editors and contributors, truthful and accurate. When possible,all facts are checked, all code is compiled. However, we are notomniscient (hell, we don’t even get paid). It is entirely possiblesomething contained within this publication is incorrect in some way.If this is the case, please drop us some email so that we can correctit in a future issue.

Also, keep in mind that Phrack Magazine accepts no responsibility forthe entirely stupid (or illegal) things people may do with theinformation contained herein. Phrack is a compendium of knowledge,wisdom, wit, and sass. We neither advocate, condone nor participatein any sort of illicit behavior. But we will sit back and watch.

Lastly, it bears mentioning that the opinions that may be expressed inthe articles of Phrack Magazine are intellectual property of their authors.These opinions do not necessarily represent those of the Phrack Staff.

#9838. Anthropic decides to go head-to-head with GTA VI release, schedules IPO for the same day

We get it, Dario - you don't want people calling out sick to play

Well, it’s official: Anthropic will become the first publicly-traded frontier AI lab in history come the opening of markets on Thursday.

The company kicked off its IPO roadshow last week, announcing plans to offer 825 million shares with an IPO price between $70 and $78 a share when sales begin Thursday.

The company's most recent SEC filing cites that price range but allows for the possibility of a higher price, which should be determined Wednesday night.

Late on Wednesday, Bloomberg reported that Anthropic would price at $83, citing people familiar. Whatever the case, Anthropic is likely to be valued at more than $1 trillion.

Anthropic’s debutante ball has been on the horizon for a while, and documents leaked in late September made it all the more inevitable as the company’s finances revved up and it sought to capture the momentum of its best quarter to date before things start to tail off.

The company revised its IPO documents on November 2, warning that the 12x growth it was touting was unlikely to continue in the long term due to compute infrastructure investments to the tune of nearly $900 billion it was on the hook for over the next few years.

"In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our revenue was $33.2 billion, representing a year-over-year growth rate of 1,206%," the revised prospectus reads. "We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all."

It’s possible, in other words, that Anthropic may never be a money maker despite the hype and its position as the first mover. The IPO prospectus is short on answers to critical questions and leaves a lot unanswered - like, for example, whether it’s going to actually be able to pay its bills.

"Our ability to meet the substantial and growing financial obligations of these requirements to secure compute depends on our ability to generate significant revenue growth," the updated prospectus admits.

Investors don’t seem to care right now, though.

Anthropic already has compute commitments amounting to roughly $70.7 billion in the next 12 months. That’s just shy of its $81 billion run-rate as of October 31.

Expect more hot air to be injected tomorrow, adding additional surface tension and the possibility of even more losses if, and when, this monster pops. ®

InfoQ Homepage News Airbnb Introduces CASTLE for Training Natural Language Search Models with Synthetic Data

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read

Airbnb researchers have introduced CASTLE, a framework designed to address the cold-start problem in natural language search. The approach uses de-identified booking sessions and large language models (LLMs) to jointly generate synthetic search queries and relevance labels, enabling model training before sufficient real search traffic is available.

Natural language search allows guests to describe their preferences in everyday language, such as "romantic cabin near skiing" or "pet-friendly beach house that sleeps eight", rather than relying exclusively on predefined filters. Training such systems presents two challenges: generating queries that reflect actual user behavior and determining which property listings are relevant to each query.

Previous approaches, including InPars and Promptagator, address query generation and relevance labeling as separate tasks. They use LLMs to generate queries from documents or examples, followed by additional model-based judgments to assign relevance labels. According to the researchers, this separation can introduce additional sources of error and differences between synthetic and real-user query distributions.

CASTLE uses contrastive listing pairs derived from de-identified booking sessions. When a guest books a property after viewing several alternatives, the selected listing becomes a positive example, while another viewed but unbooked property serves as a negative example. An LLM is then prompted to generate a query that matches the positive listing but not the negative one. This allows relevance labels to be established through the construction process rather than through a separate evaluation step.

The framework combines three query-generation strategies: template-based prompts, few-shot prompts using approximately 500 seed queries collected through targeted user research, and attribute-grounded prompts focusing on distinguishing listing characteristics. A variety mechanism also encourages variation in query length and phrasing.

For listing pairs without sufficient booking history, including newly listed properties, CASTLE uses a Virtual Judge, an LLM-based evaluator that assigns relevance labels to additional query-listing pairs. The researchers also developed CASTLE-R, a variant intended for production environments where real search traffic has started to accumulate.

In the evaluation, CASTLE achieved a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence of 1.01 against real-user query distributions, compared with 9.33 for the best baseline, Promptagator. This represents a 9.2-fold reduction in divergence. At the attribute-type level, CASTLE achieved a KL divergence of 0.08, compared with 0.09 for manually curated survey seed queries. Source: Medium Blog

The researchers also conducted a human evaluation in which three independent subject matter experts reviewed 200 sampled triplets. Agreement with CASTLE's relevance assignments ranged from 91% to 93% across the three evaluators.

The evaluation methodology also prompted discussion on LinkedIn. Mark Tsai, an AI engineer specializing in LLM fine-tuning and evaluation, raised a question about potential overlap between training and evaluation data:

Do the training and evaluation splits keep seed templates and listing IDs disjoint? For synthetic triplets, I’d compare a random split with that stricter split, then evaluate on untouched real queries. It would help separate learning reusable intent–attribute matches from recognizing familiar templates or properties.

Wendy Ran Wei, the article's author, responded that the team evaluated the model on untouched real queries and implemented leakage guardrails when constructing evaluation sets. She also clarified that the paper does not report a controlled comparison between random splits and stricter splits with disjoint seed templates and listing IDs, identifying this as a possible direction for further investigation.

#9836. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9835. For the things we can only do together - Bonfire 1.1 Release

Choose how much you want to run yourself.

Find people, answers, and tools around Bonfire.

Choose how much you want to run yourself.

Find people, answers, and tools around Bonfire.

In 1895, H. G. Wells sent a time traveller to the year 802,701, where he found childlike, carefree people living in apparent paradise, fed and clothed without ever working or thinking for it, never suspecting that people underground were toiling to provide for them, let alone why.

Half a century later, George Orwell showed how authoritarians turn care into control: the omnipresent screen, always watching and shaping us.

In 1984, Apple launched the Macintosh with an ad that borrowed Orwell's imagery, hurling a hammer through the giant screen and setting the audience free. The ad sold liberation, but three years later Apple revealed its vision for the future: the Knowledge Navigator shows a solitary professor in a spacious study, talking to a bow-tied autonomous agent on a tablet that manages his research, his calendar and his calls. Big Brother had been smashed, just to be replaced by a butler, the same screen behind a friendlier mask.

Nearly forty years on, that vision is being delivered almost shot for shot, in every chatbot, agent and AI assistant now offering to run our lives. The gadget arrived, but the life around it didn't: as one commenter under the video points out, today that professor would more likely be an untenured adjunct living in a van than a man with a study bigger than most apartments.

Anthropologist Anna Tsing describes how certain things become encoded as possible futures, and then we develop blinders, walking towards "a stereotyped dream future. And so, we stopped seeing." The personal assistant is one of those futures.

But as David Graeber put it, "the ultimate hidden truth of the world is that it is something that we make, and could just as easily make differently". Silicon Valley's future, each of us alone with our personal assistant, is only one way to make the world. We'd rather help make what the Zapatistas call "a world where many worlds fit", with the communities we care about.

The things that bring communities together are bigger than any one of us: dealing with the climate crisis, keeping a town informed, creating knowledge for everyone, helping someone through a bad year... And no digital butler can take them off our hands. It takes people who learn, rise up, organise, change their minds, regroup, get things done, celebrate, and keep showing up for each other. The things that matter most are the ones we can only do together.

The release out today is an invitation to start making other futures, together.

This release is built around one idea: equipping groups to organise, from their first conversation to their toughest decision.

A group is an online space with its own members, goals, rules and moderation team, whether it's for a project, a neighbourhood, a working group or a whole organisation. Since July's launch, we've reworked them with the communities using them, among them Jacobin's readers on jacobin.social, twelve mental health non-profits who are building Mentaal.nl, Internet Archive Europe, Fedizen by WeDistribute, and more, with Apache.be, Totnes Pulse, NRC, and openDemocracy.net among those preparing to join them. Deciding who takes part, and how, is what turns a group into a real community, so it's theirs to make.

Each group sets its own boundaries: who can find the group, who can read posts, who can join (anyone, people on its server, on request, or by invitation) and who can post (anyone, members, or only moderators). Presets make it quick to start: an open network anyone on the fediverse can join, a local community reserved for people on the same server, an announcement channel where only moderators post, or a private club whose discussions are for members only. See the new guide to groups for more.

Nobody should have to relocate just to join a conversation or participate in a community. Our plan was compatibility first: agree on a federation standard with other projects, then make groups federate.

But the communities using them told us they couldn't wait: people wanted to take part from wherever they already are, and alliances of organisations, each on their own server, including servers that federate only with each other in archipelago mode, needed groups that span all of them.

As Bert Stavenuiter of Ypsilon (one of the 12 mental health non-profits building the Mentaal.nl network) puts it: "Bonfire enables each of our organisations to run its own community, while connecting peers, families and care workers across all of them."

Public groups on one Bonfire server can now be found, joined and followed from other Bonfire servers and from fediverse apps like Mastodon, Lemmy or PieFed. Communities don't have to ask everyone to relocate to one place or one app to take part together.

Compatibility still comes first. With no standard yet, we took the long way round: we studied how many existing apps federate today, and tried to make Bonfire's groups work with them, so that we adapt to them and they don't have to adapt to us. And we're bringing what we learned along the way back to the W3C task force, so the eventual standard fits how groups already work as much as possible.

Topics were improved to help groups give every project, question or team its own space, so conversations don't get lost in the noise and newcomers can jump straight into what interests them. Topics in a public group now federate too, so people on other servers can follow and join them.

Polls come in three kinds: a quick poll for a fast read on a question, a group decision where people suggest options and then score each one, and a consensus check that shows where a group agrees and where it doesn't, with optional blocks for serious objections.

Each server, and each group, can also agree its own community rules, starting from a library of rule examples put together by researchers at Princeton.

You choose who can reach you, about what, and how: in the app, on your phone, or in an email digest that gathers what happened while you were away. Nothing here is designed to keep you scrolling: notifications are for people to reach each other.

Bonfire comes with a powerful web app that you can also install on your phone or computer as a Progressive Web App, no app store needed. But nobody should be forced to use Bonfire's interface to take part: a Mastodon-compatible API, now in beta, enables existing apps to connect to Bonfire, and a GraphQL API is open to anyone who wants to build their own app for their community.

The full list of changes is in the changelog.

New to groups? Start with our guide to groups.

To get things started, we're opening a few groups of our own, each with a mission, and you can join them from your existing fediverse account:

For what applies across all of them, the general Bonfire Networks group has sub-topics for different areas:

And why not start your own! (see the guide to running a group)

As we wrote in 2021, "Federation will be a mess. Yes, and it will be fun!" Plurality is messier than a monopoly. It's a price worth paying so that no single company controls the infrastructure our communities organise on, free to enshittify it or switch it off on a whim. What others call chaos is really diversity, and it's where our power, resilience, and beauty come from.

"Choosing Bonfire wasn't just a technical decision, it was a fundamentally political one. We wanted a platform that couldn't be switched off by a foreign government or bought out by a billionaire. That's exactly what we got: Bonfire built not simply for us, but with us, and the result belongs to our readers as much as it does to us." — Magdalena Berger, Jacobin DE

Soon, each group will be able to define roles for its members and what each one can do: who can post, who can invite, who can see things flagged for moderation, who can act on them, and who can review moderators' decisions. A tenants' union can give its "delegates" exactly the mix of permissions they need, and a food co-op can do the same for its "shift coordinators". That's why our proposal to the W3C groups task force, now included in the draft specification, doesn't define fixed roles like "admin" and "moderator". Each group states who can do what, so it can name its own roles and any app can still make sense of them. It reuses a mechanism GoToSocial introduced, which Mastodon and others use to determine who can quote a post. Federating private groups, better cross-instance moderation and moving groups between servers are among the next things to work out.

Beyond the fediverse, we're talking with bridge builders like Bridgy Fed and Kazarma so groups can reach people on ATproto and Matrix too, and communities on networks like Blacksky's Acorn can organise across networks without anyone having to move.

Thank you to everyone who chipped in towards the maintenance and groups goals in our crowdfunding, and to the communities whose co-design is carrying groups the rest of the way. If you build fediverse software, or care about groups working the same way across every app, please join the W3C task force.

Daft Punk once said that computers "could do the music instead of us", and that while "we couldn't have done our project, definitely, without technology", "we don't really feel that's where the fun is". Neither do we. Bonfire is software, of course, but communities decide what it's for, what it becomes and who it serves, and the work itself is something we share.

So bring your people. Whether you gather to learn, to rise up, to organise or to celebrate, start or join a group from the account you already have, or set up a Bonfire of your own, and make it yours.

Take your community back: bonfirenetworks.org/start

Questions, reflections, and additions are welcome. This thread is federated, so the conversation can travel beyond this page.

#9834. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎

InfoQ Homepage News Uber’s Legal AI Agent Cuts Contract Review Time by 20% with Rules and RAG

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read

Uber’s Legal Redlining Agent has reduced average contract review time by more than 20%, with 91% accuracy in AI-generated decisions, according to the company. Integrated into Microsoft Word, the agent analyzes proposed contract changes, assesses legal risks, and recommends policy-aligned responses using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), historical lawyer feedback, and deterministic rules. Lawyers retain responsibility for reviewing and approving its recommendations.

The agent identifies edits proposed by external parties, interprets their intent, compares changes with legal policies, and suggests whether to accept, reject, or modify clauses. It also generates comments explaining recommendations and flags changes requiring closer scrutiny. Uber began developing the first generation in early 2024 and piloted it with its Legal team in 2025.

High-level workflow of the Legal Redlining Add-in / Agent (Source: Uber Blog Post)

An initial RAG implementation retrieved relevant sections from legal playbooks to guide language model responses. However, the system struggled with semantic retrieval accuracy, negotiation tone, and scenarios not covered by existing examples. Uber subsequently added a feedback loop that captures lawyers’ decisions, reasoning, and final edited text.

This change allowed the agent to retrieve examples of how similar clauses had been handled rather than relying only on whether a previous recommendation was accepted or rejected. At runtime, similarity search and metadata filtering narrow thousands of historical interactions to approximately 20 candidates. A second language model-based filtering stage evaluates their relevance. Exponential decay weighting, with a configurable half-life currently set to 365 days, prioritizes recent decisions while retaining older examples. The implementation also gives domain experts control over language and negotiation style.

Uber Engineering framed the challenge in its LinkedIn post:

How can AI help streamline repetitive contract review while keeping lawyers in control?

The legal team defines the desired tone and style, while engineers maintain the prompt structure and application workflow. The architecture combines a React and TypeScript Word add-in with a Python backend orchestrated through LangGraph. Parallel workflow nodes handle intent detection, risk assessment, and policy lookup. OpenSearch stores vectorized legal rules and historical feedback, while Redis maintains session state for follow-up questions.

Legal Redlining Agent system architecture (Source: Uber Blog Post)

A deterministic rules engine enforces non-negotiable legal requirements and overrides model recommendations when a matching rule applies. Language models handle tasks requiring contextual interpretation, including clause recommendations and negotiation tone. A final verification step checks generated responses against retrieved rules.

Uber is also exploring agentic harnesses, including Claude Code and OpenCode, alongside skills to structure and automate workflows across its agentic AI efforts. The team plans to investigate legal ontologies and knowledge graphs to represent legal concepts and relationships, providing a semantic foundation for more consistent interpretation and reasoning.

#9832. Accelerating development for massive Git repositories

Android’s source code is big – the Android 17 open source release has 1,084 Git repositories, 1.62 million files, and takes 300 GB for a built workspace. Additionally, in a typical Android source tree with hardware vendor code and first-party applications, the size increases by 2-3x. Traditionally, it took over 30 minutes to fetch Android Open Source Project (AOSP) source code and well over an hour to build on even highly capable developer workstations. As software development evolved over the last 2 years, modern coding harnesses and LLMs have accelerated the development of many projects. These tools are used today for Android operating system development, but the long sync and build times make them less efficient. Both human developers and agents need quick setup, parallel workspaces, and fast build-and-test iteration times.

We built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks. ABFS is a full suite of software across a Linux kernel filesystem module, user-space daemons, and server-side infrastructure. ABFS uses content-addressability across the entire stack to lazy-load and cache source code, developer workspaces, intermediate build files, and build results.

Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:

ABFS already powers parallel workflows for developers and agents in Android, but it is designed to scale to other massive Git-based projects.

In the Android build system, developers define build rules in Blueprint files (Android.bp), Soong compiles them into Ninja files, and Ninja executes the final build graph (see the Android build overview). Similar to the Make build tool, Ninja is timestamp-based. If a build step’s input file is newer than the existing output file, Ninja rebuilds the output file.

Analyzing the AOSP code for Android 17 shows the sheer disk footprint and file count involved in a single checkout and build.

In a typical Android tree that includes hardware-specific repositories, board support packages, first-party applications, form-factor-specific code, etc., the code size is 2–3 times the size of AOSP (over 3,000 Git repositories), compounded across multiple active SKU and legacy maintenance branches.

Building the Cuttlefish emulator target executes a build graph with 192,249 Ninja actions. While local incremental builds are fast once a tree is already built, every new workspace, branch switch, or ephemeral agent session starts cold.Even though typical developer changes touch only 1-10 different Git projects, someone building locally without any remote execution might waste up to 80 minutes on a 64-core machine repeating work their CI system already built. Even if a developer edits a core library like system/libbase, 97% of the build graph is identical to the CI build.

Sharing cached build outputs across CI and local machines is also tricky in a codebase of Android's age and rate of change. Build rules occasionally introduce hidden dependencies (such as passing an undeclared schema file inside raw compiler flags), over-declared inputs, or undeclared outputs. In timestamp-based builds, hidden dependencies silently produce stale incremental artifacts, forcing developers to wipe output directories and run clean builds.

ABFS makes building Android fast by replacing massive local source checkouts with a virtual, content-addressable filesystem (CASFS). ABFS streams files on demand only when a build actually touches them and utilizes shared build caching to help eliminate redundant downloads and compilation.

On the server side, Git-pushers continuously ingest new Git objects from Gerrit or other Git hosts into a horizontally scalable gRPC ABFS Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) Server that indexes Git content, workspace snapshots, and build step results. On the developer host, a local Least Recently Used (LRU) Cacheman daemon, Mount Daemon, and Tap utility connect user-space build tools to the kernel filesystem so checkouts and builds stream only what they need. See the full ABFS architecture on GitHub.

At the core of the client is a virtual filesystem called Content-Addressable Storage Filesystem (CASFS), a Linux kernel module that exposes Git SHA content hashes via extended attributes. When a file's hash is set, CASFS populates its metadata immediately and downloads file bytes via Cacheman only when needed:

Initial checkouts download only lightweight directory metadata prepopulated with Git hashes. CASFS uses Git's object model natively, allowing standard git and repo operations to work transparently.

CASFS can also tap build processes. Tapping records every file actually read, written, or deleted into lists called patches, which are stored alongside cached build outputs. Ninja-go replaces timestamp checks with two-phase content-addressable caching:

Ninja-go accelerates Ninja-based builds like Android and Chrome; other build systems can integrate with ABFS's caching APIs using the same model (see the two-phase caching walkthrough on GitHub).

Each mounted checkout attaches to a persistent workspace that eagerly syncs modified files, git state, and repo state through Cacheman to the ABFS CAS Server—keeping mounts synchronized across sessions or across multiple developer hosts.
