#9801. Java4Shell: Write once, RCE everywhere

A memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. A remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, read it in the style of Heartbleed, and reach remote code execution.

Begin ↓ Technical write-up ↘ Check your servers ↘ Recommendations ↘

After we disclosed PHP2Shell, we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java.

Today, we are disclosing Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the most popular Java runtime. Under CVSS 4.0, this vulnerability scores 9.2 out of 10 (CRITICAL).

While PHP is a high-level web technology, Java sits much deeper. Java is the world's third most popular programming language, powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies. It is the beating heart of the modern economy. Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems.

Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages. To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:

In older OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 128 of A followed by =.

Our initial testing demonstrated remote code execution in the following widely deployed Java applications, in their default configs.

The lists are non-exhaustive. We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested. samczsun also shared a client-side exploit with us. A Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own.

Here are a demo video of the exploits running:

Memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the Internet. But one of Java's biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers' behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software.

But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life.

To speed up Base64 decoding, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors. The bug sits in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters. For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array. After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array. Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted.

As with PHP2Shell, Calif used AI to find and weaponize Java4Shell. AI brings the horsepower. Our researchers bring the context. The best hacker today is neither AI nor human. It is the centaur hacker, part human, part AI.

It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit. The total token cost was less than $200.

One thing to note about this vulnerability is that there is no universal exploit. Depending on how Base64 is used and how the application works, different steps may be required for exploitation. Calif was able to accelerate the exploit development by spending initial effort building pipelines and strategies, then directing AI agents to use those for initial exploitation. Afterwards, most of the later chains are built almost autonomously with AI.

Java is one of many shared software stacks we all rely on. Over the years, it has grown to serve many different needs. Each feature request may make sense on its own, but everyone inherits the added complexity. Those who need a feature get the benefit. Everyone else carries the code and its risks, even if they never use it.

Java4Shell is a concrete example. The Base64 optimization helps applications that decode enormous amounts of data. But the code ships to everyone else too, including applications that gain little from it. On affected systems, an optimization few applications needed became a serious security risk.

Features can be useful, and most bugs can be fixed. But why do we have to worry about code we never needed in the first place?

If you don't need something, there is little reason to keep it running in your systems. Do you need that hand-rolled assembly Base64 decoder to process a few hundred bytes? Probably not.

Earlier this year we found Squidbleed, an older cousin of Heartbleed, hiding in the Squid proxy since 1997. The bug was in Squid's FTP module. But who uses FTP anymore? It's a dead protocol and should be removed.

Removing code is harder than it sounds. An apparently unused feature may have hidden dependencies. Someone has to understand what can be removed, make the change, and test what remains.

This is where AI can help to make that work practical at a scale we could not previously afford.

The same centaur hacker that discovered PHP2Shell and Java4Shell can comb a large codebase and flag dead code, bloated features, and needless optimizations. We call this vibe-uncoding: identify the parts a system actually needs, then remove everything else to reduce its attack surface.

With AI, everyone is asking, “What can we build?” But maybe the right question for security is, “What can we delete?”

On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution.

A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode.

Complicated system interactions are hard, and this complexity can make exploiting hard bugs easy.

After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into some thing completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway.

Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues.

Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder...

Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold?

That sheer persistence is prompting AI and ignoring slops for around 20 minutes, by the way.

The issue lies in OpenJDK HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. C2 is the most aggressive JIT compiler in the Java Virtual Machine. Specifically, if you trigger a function repeatedly, then it will compile that function into native code. Even then, ordinary native code itself is not fast enough. Modern CPUs have specialized instructions that allow processing data even faster. HotSpot uses them in optimized routines called intrinsics. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write.

The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic iterates through the input in 256-byte blocks; if it is less than 256, then it will do so in 64-byte blocks. When the input is less than 64 bytes, it uses evmovdqub, the intrinsic for the VMOVDQU8 instruction. This instruction takes a 64-bit mask that decides which bytes are read from or written to memory. The mask is first calculated from the input and output length, then updated to reflect the number of padding bytes ('=') in the Base64-encoded string. This is shown in the following (pseudocode):

In the above code, if the remaining input is of the form =, ==, X=, X==, XY=, or ===, then output_len will be computed as zero. However, since there is padding, output_len is decremented, resulting in an underflowed value of -1 or -2. Since bzhiq(-1, output_len) doesn’t change any bits if output_len >= 64, this results in output_mask == -1u64.

Later the code uses evmovdqub to read and write multiple bytes at a time. For a write, if the mask bit is 1, the byte at that index in the vector register is written to memory. So when output_mask == -1u64, all 64 bytes are written during the following operation:

The generated stub returns the number of bytes it successfully decoded, and returns early when it detects invalid input. The remaining bytes are handled by the Java code, which throws IllegalArgumentException if the input is invalid.

At runtime, the decoded buffer length is calculated as (ceil(inp_len / 4) * 3) - padding. When the bug is triggered, with 65 bytes ([64 bytes] + '=') as input, that calculation allocates a 50-byte buffer. During decoding the bug makes output_mask == -1 for evmovdqub, so 64 bytes are written starting at offset 48, an out-of-bounds write past the end of the buffer.

On OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 'A' * 128 + '=' instead of 'A' * 64 + '=', because the length threshold to reach the code path is higher.

The Base64 bug was gold, but not the type that sits on the riverbed waiting to be panned out. It was the type that was deep, dark, and hard to access. While we had memory corruption, exploiting it looked difficult, perhaps even borderline unexploitable, since it only wrote fixed bytes to the heap. Only the landing position of the out-of-bounds write is controllable.

We get the following 64 bytes write starting from the position in buffer where the remaining sets of Base64 decoded bytes would have been written to:

The uncontrolled out-of-bounds write turned out not to be a big problem. We reused a common JavaScript engine exploitation primitive, the classic technique of overwriting a buffer length.

We call the buffer whose length we overwrite the writer. Once its length is corrupted, it keeps accepting our chosen bytes, so if we place another array or object after it, we can corrupt that neighbor with all of our chosen values. That upgrades the fixed write into a bounded, chosen-value linear write.

If we then corrupt another array's length and its data is copied back into the response, we have built a heap disclosure primitive, the reader, from the out-of-bounds read. At this point, before any code execution, we already had JavaBleed, the ability to leak contents from the Java heap, which may hold PII, private keys, other secret keys, and tokens.

From the writer and reader, the rest of this write-up builds the full attack. We repair the objects the linear write damaged to keep the JVM running, mount data-only attacks on application logic, and escalate the bounded write into arbitrary writes that reach the Code Cache and JVM hooks for code execution.

But first things first, we need to align the heap to our advantage.

Other alignments conceptually exist (e.g. type confusion, registers control from GC itself). Due to time constraints, we have not researched them deeply, and this strategy generalized well enough for our cases. Give us a shout if you invent something new.

G1 divides the heap into fixed-size regions. Before the region arithmetic matters, the critical arrays have to leave their threads' private allocation ranges.

HotSpot normally gives each Java thread a thread-local allocation buffer (TLAB), a private slice of Eden. Objects created by different request threads advance different cursors, which gives us no useful order between a Base64 decoder in one TLAB and a writer in another.

The first grooming layer controls the allocation route. The critical array's size and the space left in the worker's TLAB decide whether HotSpot refills that TLAB or takes the attacker-preferred outside-TLAB allocation path.

The second layer controls the layout. However, we do not choose how G1 allocates memory, and we don't know the current heap state. To approach this limitation, Calif used the tried and tested method of Spray and Pray.

Object sizes and padding fix offsets inside region-sized spans. We spray several live writer and reader pairs to give the decoder output several possible neighbors. When its region lands immediately below a writer region, the widened reader produces a larger application response. We discard misses and retry until successful.

One early challenge during exploit development was that the AI would get stuck during heap grooming primitive development. In order to save tokens and time, Calif wrote a small heap tracer and visualizer to give the agent information about the heap state, combined with our expertise on specific cases.

In order to perform remote grooming, each request data would be sent up until the critical heap allocation would occur. By ensuring the data that was previously sent had a TCP acknowledgement, the exploit would have control over the allocations up to date. Once we were confident our data so far is buffered on the target, we then sent the rest, completing the http request. This allows both heap allocation control and more precise schedule as delivering small network packets is more stable than big ones.

The exact allocation and free order schedule belongs to the targeted application profile, while we are able to control the adding, writer, reader, and decoder pieces.

The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.

To summarize the chain so far, we will warm up the Base64 decoder to C2 tier. We can rehearse the exploit run to calibrate timing and responses against the target before causing corruption to occur. Once the required information has been obtained, we can trigger the vulnerability. Incorrect placement could cause the JVM to crash, but in many instances, we can simply try again.

Request streaming. Some current grooming profiles need partial request bodies to reach the application. A proxy that waits for the complete body removes their release timing. nginx buffers request bodies by default.

Request buffering is not a general mitigation. Elasticsearch runs from one complete request, so this setting does not stop that chain. After a configured WebSocket upgrade, later frames pass through a tunnel and request-body buffering no longer applies to them.

Application profiles. There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot.

Here is a self-contained proof of concept. It warms the Base64 decoder until the vulnerable intrinsic is used, then decodes the malformed 64 × "A" + "=" input into a 4096-byte array. On an affected JDK it prints REPRODUCED: the decoder rejects the input, but 62 bytes (offsets 50 to 111) past the decoded output have already been overwritten. Every write lands inside a real array, so the trigger is safe to run.

We are holding back the application-specific exploits for now. This write-up covers the vulnerability and the general exploitation technique. The weaponized chains for individual products stay private until everyone has had a chance to upgrade. We will publish them later.

Java4Shell affects OpenJDK from version 17.0.6 or newer.

Because they are built from OpenJDK, the following Java distributions are also vulnerable:

According to Oracle, the following Oracle Java SE versions are vulnerable: 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3. We thank Oracle for providing this information ahead of publication time.

Because the vulnerable code is hardware-specific, Java4Shell also requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support. ARM64 CPUs are not affected.

These mainstream CPU families meet the hardware requirements:

All Java users should update immediately.

InfoQ Homepage News Datadog Brings Production Experimentation to AI Agent Observability

Nov 17, 2026 3 min read

Datadog is extending its Agent Observability platform with Online Experiments, allowing engineering teams to compare AI agent versions against real production traffic rather than relying exclusively on predefined evaluation datasets. The capability combines agent evaluation scores with operational measurements such as latency, token consumption, execution cost, and errors, helping teams establish whether changes to models, prompts, retrieval strategies, or tools actually improve an agent.

The announcement addresses a growing challenge in agent development: a change that performs better in a controlled test may behave very differently when exposed to unpredictable user requests. Datadog's approach brings controlled experimentation, production telemetry, and execution traces together, giving teams evidence of both the outcome and the behaviour behind it.

Offline evaluations remain an important part of agent development. Teams can run different versions against predefined datasets, assess responses and identify known regressions before deployment.

However, these evaluations are only as representative as the datasets and scoring criteria behind them. New user workflows, unexpected requests, and changing tool responses can expose weaknesses that existing test cases never anticipated.

Online experiments address this limitation by evaluating agent behaviour against real user interactions. Teams can compare a control version with a modified variant by randomly distributing production traffic between them, reducing the influence of differences in user requests.

This provides a more realistic view of how an agent performs under actual workloads, while also helping teams identify new scenarios that should eventually become part of their offline regression datasets.

Datadog integrates its Agent Observability evaluators with its Experiments capability, allowing evaluation scores to be compared alongside conventional operational metrics.

Teams can measure response quality, accuracy, and completeness while tracking execution duration, token consumption, estimated cost, and workflow errors. Feature Flags manage traffic allocation, letting engineers expose a change to a small percentage of users before rolling it out more widely.

This is important because improvements rarely come without trade-offs. A cheaper model might require more retries, while a revised retrieval strategy could improve evidence quality but increase execution time.

Datadog also connects experiment results to individual agent traces. Engineers can inspect tool calls, supplied arguments, and returned results to understand why a particular variant behaved differently.

According to the article, the experiment compared GPT-5.6 Luna against GPT-6 Luna, splitting traffic evenly between the two. An LLM-based evaluator scored investigation quality from one to five, considering accuracy, completeness, and whether conclusions were supported by available evidence.

They claim the results showed a 44.3% reduction in estimated cost for the newer model, with quality scores remaining close at 3.84 and 3.86, respectively.

However, the operational results revealed potential concerns. The newer model showed estimated increases in execution duration and workflow errors, although the confidence intervals were too broad to establish definitive regressions.

Inspecting the traces revealed that the newer model also supplied invalid tool parameters more frequently, usually recovering after retries. This behaviour was not sufficiently visible in the overall quality score.

Datadog used that finding to improve tool handling before proceeding with the model change. The failed calls also provided candidates for additional offline regression tests.

Datadog is not alone in trying to solve this challenge. Tools such as LangSmith and Langfuse provide agent tracing and evaluation capabilities, while experimentation platforms such as LaunchDarkly support controlled feature rollouts. Datadog's approach connects these concerns within its existing observability ecosystem, linking evaluation results directly to production experiments and execution evidence.

Datadog's broader proposition is that online experiments can create a feedback loop between production behaviour and development testing. Unexpected failures become new regression cases, while subsequent experiments establish whether changes actually resolve them.

The important shift is from asking whether an agent passes a predefined evaluation to establishing whether it performs better under real conditions. For agent engineering, production experimentation may become as important as traditional software testing.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

#9798. IPv6 delegation, an unusually subtle failure mode

Running a custom x64 router has a lot of upsides. One, it runs mainline Linux, so it gets updates quickly. Two, router adblocking. 'Nuff said. And three, if something breaks, you get to dive in deep and figure out what's going wrong.

This week, I had a really interesting time with my custom setup. I noticed that if I'd restart pppd (which connects to my ISP), Google would stop working. It would still resolve, but I couldn't reach it.

I have a stack where networkd is responsible for the network in general, with pppd dialing in to my ISP, kea-dhcp4 handing out DHCPv4 addresses, blocky handling DNS (on the router as well as the laptop) and networkd itself handling RA. As far as I knew, there was nothing wrong in this stack at all. All the daemons themselves are battle-tested and known to be working fine.

So maybe this was a problem with my laptop?

One ping told me that Google was getting resolved to its IPv6 address, which exonerated DNS, but I couldn't ping it. An IPv4 address on the other hand, worked fine.

On the other hand, wlan0 showed 2 groups of IPv6 addresses with the older IPv6 address having a preferred lifetime greater than 0. Could this be the culprit? I restarted NetworkManager, and lo and behold, Google magically started working again and I was down to just one group of IPv6 addresses, the newer ones.

I've never debugged networks in depth, but the problem here seemed to be fairly simple to grasp. Whenever pppd restarts, it negotiates a new connection with my ISP, which provides a new prefix to my router for delegation. However, no device drops the old IPv6 address. At first I thought this was NetworkManager's fault, but then I saw my iPhone do the same thing. Two points don't make a pattern, but they do make a line. Which pointed straight at networkd.

Don't get me wrong. I like networkd. The only reason I have NetworkManager on my laptop is because it's purpose built for Wi-Fi and roaming and it's never let me down yet (iwd ftw). My router and server both run networkd. It's a very comfortable, no-nonsense daemon. So I was reluctant to blame it. So I turned to pppd instead as a cop-out.

I decided to ensure that pppd would never restart when I'd redeploy my NixOS router. But unfortunately, I've had times when my ISP has randomly hiccoughed and pppd reconnects to it leading to the same problem all over again. Which meant I'd have to get to the bottom of this.

A little bit of searching led me to RFC 9096, Improving the Reaction of Customer Edge Routers to IPv6 Renumbering Events, which tightens RFC 7084, Basic Requirements for IPv6 Customer Edge Routers. Basically, whenever a new prefix is given to the router and the old one dropped by upstream, the router needs to advertise the old prefix with preferred and valid lifetimes of 0 which causes consumers of the router advertisement to stop using it as a source address.

Interestingly, networkd has an issue RFC 7084 support in networkd (automatic ipv6 range delegation) where a requirement for properly implementing RFC 9096 came up in September 2026. There's a patch as well which hasn't yet been merged. The same issue has been brought up with radvd on OPNsense and closed as "not planned", as well as with dnsmasq on OPNsense. VyOS's dynamic-prefix support is still an open request. Which meant that the usual suspects were out. There's only one option left, and it's not available on NixOS. odhcpd from OpenWrt, which actually does implement RFC 9096.

I was a bit wary of relying on an OpenWrt package. Not because I think there's anything wrong with OpenWrt (quite the contrary!), but because the distribution itself is unusual. It doesn't use systemd or dbus, instead using procd as pid1 and uses ubus for IPC. I know that many of their packages depend on these two pieces of infrastructure to function, so that was the first thing I checked. Fortunately, odhcpd is unusual in that it can get information from the kernel directly through netlink and can be configured without the need for ubus, so that was not a blocker. Packaging it took me a while, but I submitted it for review to nixpkgs and began running it on my router, switching off router advertisement on networkd. I could have used odhcpd for DHCP as well, but I was fairly happy with kea-dhcp4 so I left it alone.

And lo and behold, when I deliberately restarted pppd, I got:

Success! The best thing was that odhcpd's memory is persistent across reboots and is agnostic to the time set on your machine. This is pretty important for me, because I haven't replaced the dead CMOS battery on my router and the clock resets every time the router restarts. This allows odhcpd to advertise old prefixes with the correct preferred/valid lifetime of 0 after every reboot without caring about when they were delegated. In practice, this would matter if my router loses power while my Wi-Fi access point remains up, or if I reboot my router (which definitely does happen often). Given my family's reliance on the home network remaining up, I'd rather cover all cases.

My euphoria lasted until I got onto my iPhone, where the old address lingered on my screen. I switched off mobile data to check (iOS silently routes to mobile data where Wi-Fi fails, a service called Wi-Fi Assist) and the same problem persisted for a few minutes before the address changed and the problem resolved on its own.

Took me a bit of packet capture to work out, but it became clear what had happened. The router advertisement had gone out as soon as the prefix had arrived, but the phone was sleeping and missed it. It caught the next advertisement when it was awake and in my hands. This shows us that dropping prefixes is prompt, but not instant. It took around 10 minutes for my phone to pick the new one up. networkd advertises times of 30/60 mins for preferred/valid respectively, while radvd advertises times of 4/24 hours by default. odhcpd conforms to the recommendations of RFC 9096 by advertising 45/90 mins.

odhcpd behaves slightly differently from its natural home in OpenWrt when deployed on another distribution. It cannot be updated via ubus (note: it technically can because ubus is packaged in NixOS, but I wasn't using it here) so it can only get interface names at startup and it gets state by talking to the kernel, not from ubus. The NixOS module ties it to device units so that it picks them up at startup. It also differs quite a bit from networkd's behaviour. For example, networkd, reloading its config, would send a router-lifetime-0 goodbye message, which odhcpd doesn't (which is correct here, because odhcpd being down does not imply the router being down). This would cause a brief network disruption where for a moment, everything connected to my network would lose IPv6 capability momentarily as networkd reloaded. And finally, when pppd would go down, odhcpd advertises a router lifetime of 0, implying there's no default route available, telling clients to not use it as a gateway.

The takeaway for me was quite simple. I usually prefer using systemd utilities wherever possible. I prefer networkd, I don't use a separate syslog daemon, I feel like udev is my friend, and so on. However, that holds true when the machine is a client. As soon as the machine has to behave as a server to another machine, I'd prefer to fall back to specialised tools. Hence, my router has chrony instead of systemd-timesyncd, blocky instead of systemd-resolved, and kea-dhcp4 and now odhcpd in place of systemd-networkd's DHCP and router advertisement functionality. There's enough edge cases that getting dedicated tools there just makes more sense.

But more than that, I heartily recommend odhcpd. I don't know whether I'd want to replace kea-dhcp4 with it or not, but as a router advertisement daemon it's the best one I've found for a home network connecting to a consumer ISP.

#9797. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

#9796. [$] Zellij manages terminal workspaces with style

Zellij is a relatively new entrant in the terminal-multiplexer category. Like GNU Screen and tmux it gives users the ability to manage a workspace inside a terminal with split panes, provides session management, and so forth; but Zellij also includes a web server for browser access to a terminal session, is extensible via a plugin API, and is likely more beginner-friendly than its predecessors. Its most recent release, version 0.46, adds a standalone terminal emulator, a built-in inbox for notifications, and a settings screen so users can configure the application without fussing with configuration files. While the low version number might suggest that it is not yet ready for serious use, it seems stable and full-featured enough to meet the needs of many users.

#9795. Redict deprecated in favor of Valkey

Drew DeVault has announced that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated. He recommends switching to Valkey, the permissively licensed Redis fork supported by the Linux Foundation. The two projects are mutually compatible, so switching should be as simple as changing which package is installed and renaming the configuration file.

I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose. However, with the valkey project's success, and Redis's return to a copyleft license, Redict was not able to build a sustainable community.

We recommend that Redict users switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects. We advise against switching back to Redis; though it is once again open source, and copyleft, it uses a contributor license agreement which will facilitate another rug-pull when Redis has a bad financial quarter.

#9794. The Magic of Partial Evaluation

There are certain ideas in software that are simply beautiful. It doesn't matter if they have any practical use. It doesn't matter that you will never convince your coworkers to consider them. There is just something captivating about the way some computational systems work.

For me, the most beautiful pieces of software are those that reveal something about the nature of programming languages. Programming languages are my obsession. I have never met a problem that couldn't be solved by introducing yet another programming language. Solving a problem at the programming language level is about solving the meta problem. Instead of trying to solve a particular problem, we take a step back and ask how we can solve a whole class of problems at once.

So when I find something that makes me rethink the nature of programming languages, I start rethinking computation as a whole. One of these incredibly beautiful but tricky concepts goes by the name partial evaluation. If you are fascinated by interpreters and compilers, partial evaluation will teach you how they are related, and how you can get a compiler for free.

Partial evaluation has been a fascination of mine for a while. But this whole thing came up when James Long announced he had revived Meta's partial evaluator for JavaScript called prepack. When I first heard about prepack, I had some high hopes and expectations for the project, but was sadly let down. This revival brought to light those same dreams. But sadly, just as with the original aim, prepack was not designed for beauty, but for practicality. So I figured it was time to renew my own efforts.

Yes, in some ways this is a post repping my own library I'm releasing. But I'm not doing this because I want it to be used. I'm doing this because it lets you play with the idea I find so beautiful. That is what this post is about.

As a person who reads code, you can think about how this code computes and what answer it will give. But you can do more than just give the answer. You can see the expanded form of this particular code for these particular calls. This code is spiritually the same as the following expression, once we expand it out.

In this case, there is really nothing at all that this code needs to do at runtime. A sufficiently smart compiler will just run this code directly at compile time and give the answer. But this is a bit less clear if things come in at runtime.

It might seem like we can't do anything here, but again, if you are used to thinking about how programs run, you can trace this out and realize this is just the same as:

What we have done in both of these cases is called partial evaluation. In the first, it was a trivial case because everything was statically known. But in this latter case, we have reduced a program down into the essentials of its dynamic structure. There are no recursive function calls left. All of this has been expanded as far as it could till we get just the dynamic parts of the code remaining.

This intuitive notion of partial evaluation is all you need to know to appreciate the beauty here. Partial evaluation just evaluates the part of the program we can evaluate at build time and leaves all the rest. When we do this with certain programs in certain combinations, we get some quite surprising, incredible behavior.

Here we have a very simple interpreter for a language that just supports arithmetic. For the above expression, you should be able to think about how we could start "partially" evaluating it. (In this case, it can be a full evaluation.) If this kind of partial evaluation isn't quite clicking for you, I've put the steps below to hopefully help it make sense.

This is a simple evaluation of the code. But what happens if we throw a value we don't know into the expression?

Here we can see that clear partial evaluation difference. We don't know how to evaluate Number(process.argv[2]). We have no idea what the answer to that will be. But as part of this process, we do know some partial information about it. For example, when we get to

we know that Number(process.argv[2]) is indeed a number. So we can partially evaluate it further. Hopefully this is all making sense. But if you are like me, this all might seem a bit trivial and uninteresting. So let's look at a more complicated example.

Here we have a brainfuck interpreter. And the example program we want to partially evaluate does not require any input at all (in brainfuck , is the way you get input). So when we go to partially evaluate this, we will just get an answer. In this case, this program is actually brainfuck's "hello world". But what about a program with input?

When we do our partial evaluation, we get the following:

What is this? A compiled brainfuck program! This is the first incredible fact: when you take an interpreter and partially evaluate it with a program, you get the compiled program out! Now this particular exact form is an artifact of how my partial evaluator works. You could imagine slightly different code. But the key is that what we've done is remove the interpreter completely.

What we've discovered here is the first of three so-called Futamura Projections. Our partial evaluator, when applied to an interpreter and given a program, can give us a compiled version of that program. Or to put it in pseudocode.

Depending on your exposure to interpreters and compilers, this might seem miraculous or mundane. Writing an interpreter and writing a compiler can seem like significantly different undertakings. In the age of AI, perhaps less so, but I think even then many things still hold. It is quite easy to instrument an interpreter, quite a bit harder to do so for a compiler. Changing an interpreter to support new features is quite easy, less so for a compiler. But more than that, there are all sorts of things that can be thought of as interpreters, that we'd almost never write a compiler for.

Consider this simple schema setup. This is code that can easily be partially evaled into something where we have created specialized functions for our particular schema. While not the most crucial code, this can give us a 5x performance boost when our objects start getting more complicated. You may think that we should just hand-write those functions. Or hand-write a compiler for these schemas. But what about those schemas that exist only at runtime? Now we either need to compile those on the fly, or we have to keep both a compiler and interpreter. Having a way to partial eval lowers this burden quite a bit.

But if the Futamura projections stopped here, they would be exciting, but not quite the craziness they are. To understand how this can go further, we are going to take this a step beyond your raw intuition of what it means to partially evaluate something and give a different frame. We can think of partial evaluation as a process of "specializing" a program.

What exactly is specializing a program? Well, it is taking a program that is generic and making a version that instead works for a single program. Let's think about a simple pattern matcher program like an overly simplified regex.

This program is generic. It lets you match on many different patterns. That can be great if we need that flexibility. But if you don't have a bunch of patterns, it might be worth it to just make specialized code. Now, exactly what kind of specialized code? It might be that you only have this literal pattern; then you want to specialize very particularly.

Or you just have *** as a pattern.

For any bit of generic code, we can think of how to move our code to a more specialized form.

Partial evaluation is a form of specialization that figures out what it should specialize on based on what input is static and what is dynamic. In many ways, a partial evaluator is a generic specializer. Given any program, we can make a specialized version of it for any input. What happens if we specialize an interpreter for a given input? We get back that interpreter for only exactly that one program. But what do we need then? Do we need all this generic dispatch? No, we know the full program. We don't need any operations we don't actually use. We can fully get rid of all the generic interpreter mechanism.

But if the specializer can specialize any program, can it specialize itself?

This leads us to the second Futamura projection. Put in our pseudo-code format, we get:

Or, to put it in our specializer language, what if we make a special version of our generic specializer? What is it specialized for? A particular interpreter. Now we have a function that, given any program, will spit out newly specialized interpreters just for that program. Or, in Java speak, we have a specialized interpreter factory.

Let's see a real example of one of these compilers to make this concrete. Here is the interpreter we are going to specialize.

When we apply our second projection, we get out the following compiler:

And if we compile one of these very simple programs, we can see the output:

Now, of course, this is not a very interesting language. But hopefully you can see this general idea. Given an interpreter, we automatically derive a compiler! Pretty incredible.

But we can't stop at the second projection. We have to push on and get to the final mind-bending projection. If you apply our specializer to itself as input, you get a compiler generator.

So now we have a generic function that will spit out compilers for any interpreter we give it!

I have implemented a reasonable, but still very limited partial evaluator for JavaScript in Rust. I have taken it further to try to make it work quite well for a number of different interpreters and interpreter-like programs in JavaScript. I've also tried to get limited versions of the second and third projections working. Go play with it, see what works, what doesn't, file issues, or better, use some of your tokens to help me make more cases work.

But most of all, explore. This is such a rich space. Below are some papers, blogs, and projects about partial evaluation in some way, shape, or form. There has never been a better time to play with these kinds of crazy techniques for programming languages. Don't let what is practical stop you from exploring the cool, interesting aspects of programming.

#9793. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#9789. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.
